params.question: Haptens such as penicillin can trigger a full immune response on their own because they bind specifically to antibodies.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: A hapten such as penicillin can bind antibodies but cannot trigger a full immune response on its own because it lacks the size and complexity needed to recruit T-cell help. It must couple to a carrier protein to become immunogenic.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Although haptens bind to antibodies, they are too small to trigger an immune response alone. A hapten must first couple to a carrier protein — like penicillin binding to serum albumin — to become a complete immunogen.

interactions.label: The complement system can be activated through three distinct pathways — classic

params.question: The complement system can be activated through three distinct pathways — classical, lectin, and alternative. At which step do all three pathways converge?

answers.text: Binding of C1q to the antibody–antigen complex

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: C1q binding initiates only the classical pathway. The lectin and alternative pathways use entirely different triggers.
Mannose-binding lectin activates only the lectin pathway by recognising sugar residues on microbial surfaces — it does not trigger the classical or alternative pathways.

answers.text: Cleavage of C3, producing the opsonin C3b

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. All three complement pathways converge at C3. Cleavage generates C3b, a potent opsonin that coats pathogens for phagocytosis and also drives assembly of the membrane attack complex (C5b–C9) downstream.
The membrane attack complex forms downstream of C3 cleavage, as the terminal effector of the cascade — not the convergence point of the three initiating pathways.

overallFeedback.feedback: All three complement pathways converge at C3. The cleavage product C3b is the key opsonin, and drives formation of the downstream membrane attack complex.
Excellent. C3 is the hub of complement activation — C3b opsonises pathogens, and the cascade proceeds to form the membrane attack complex.

interactions.label: A healthcare worker receives a Mantoux tuberculin skin test. After 48 hours, an

params.question: A healthcare worker receives a Mantoux tuberculin skin test. After 48 hours, an induration of 16 mm is observed at the injection site. Which immunological mechanism produces this reaction?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IgE-mediated reactions (Type I hypersensitivity) produce symptoms within minutes, not after 48 hours. The delayed onset of the Mantoux response rules out this mechanism.
Complement and neutrophil recruitment are features of Type II and Type III hypersensitivity. The Mantoux reaction is T-cell mediated, with no role for antibodies.

answers.text: Natural killer cells recognising tuberculin as a foreign protein

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Natural killer cells are innate immune cells that do not require prior sensitisation. The Mantoux test detects adaptive T-cell memory from previous mycobacterial exposure.

answers.text: Sensitised Th1 cells releasing interferon-gamma and activating macrophages

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Mantoux test is a Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction. Previously sensitised CD4+ Th1 cells recognise mycobacterial antigens, release IFN-γ, and activate macrophages — producing the characteristic induration at 48–72 hours.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Mantoux reaction is a Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity response. Sensitised Th1 cells release IFN-γ, activating macrophages over 48–72 hours — no antibody is involved.
Spot on. The Mantoux test reads out Th1 cell-mediated memory — a classic example of Type IV delayed hypersensitivity.

interactions.label: A nurse develops acute bronchospasm, urticaria, and hypotension within minutes o

params.question: A nurse develops acute bronchospasm, urticaria, and hypotension within minutes of receiving a routine antibiotic injection. Which Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity type explains this reaction?

answers.text: Type II — IgG or IgM antibodies destroy the patient's own cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Type II (cytotoxic) hypersensitivity involves antibodies targeting cell-surface antigens, as in ABO-incompatible transfusion reactions — not the acute systemic collapse seen here.

answers.text: Type I — antigen cross-links IgE on mast cells, triggering histamine release

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This is Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity. On re-exposure, the drug antigen cross-links IgE already bound to mast cell surfaces, causing rapid degranulation and massive histamine release — producing anaphylaxis within minutes.

answers.text: Type III — immune complexes deposit in vessel walls and activate complement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Type III hypersensitivity develops over hours and causes localised tissue inflammation through immune-complex deposition — as in lupus nephritis. It does not cause acute anaphylaxis.

answers.text: Type IV — sensitised T cells release interferon-gamma over 24–72 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Type IV is a delayed response (24–72 hours) mediated by T cells, not antibodies. The Mantoux test and contact dermatitis are classic examples — onset within minutes rules this out.

overallFeedback.feedback: Anaphylaxis developing within minutes of drug exposure is the hallmark of Type I hypersensitivity: IgE cross-linking on mast cells triggers immediate histamine release.
Exactly. Type I hypersensitivity — IgE cross-linking on mast cells, histamine release, anaphylaxis within minutes — is the mechanism in this clinical scenario.

interactions.label: A renal transplant recipient maintained on cyclosporin develops a skin malignanc

params.question: A renal transplant recipient maintained on cyclosporin develops a skin malignancy three years after transplantation. Which immunological principle best explains this increased cancer risk?

answers.text: The transplanted kidney produced tumour-promoting growth factors

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Transplanted organs do not produce tumour-promoting factors. The increased cancer risk results from systemic immunosuppression, not from the graft itself.

answers.text: HLA mismatch between donor and recipient triggered malignant transformation of host cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HLA mismatch drives graft rejection, not malignant transformation. The cancer arises from mutations in the recipient's own cells that escape immune detection.

answers.text: Cyclosporin-mediated suppression of immune surveillance allowed nascent tumour cells to escape destruction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Burnet's immune surveillance theory holds that the immune system continuously eliminates nascent cancers. Cyclosporin blocks calcineurin, suppressing IL-2 production and T-cell activation — this impairs surveillance and allows tumour cells to proliferate unchecked.

answers.text: Preformed antibodies against donor HLA cross-reacted with the patient's skin cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Preformed anti-donor antibodies cause hyperacute graft rejection within minutes of transplantation — they do not cause skin malignancies years later.

overallFeedback.feedback: Burnet's immune surveillance theory explains this: the immune system normally destroys nascent tumour cells. Cyclosporin suppresses T-cell activation, impairing this surveillance and increasing cancer risk.
Correct. Immunosuppression disables the immune surveillance that normally eliminates nascent cancers — a direct consequence of Burnet's theory applied to transplant medicine.
